div.head: Background & Summary
div.p: Brain tumors, characterized by abnormal cell growth within the central nervous system (CNS), pose significant health risks, leading to neurological dysfunction. e World Health Organization classification for primary CNS neoplasms (WHO CNS 5) combines histopathology and molecular biomarkers for integrated diagnostics 1 . In India, CNS tumor incidence ranges between 5 and 10 per 100,000 people, influenced by genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors 2,3 . Glial tumors, particularly astrocytoma, glioblastoma, and oligodendroglioma, are the most prevalent, with glioblastoma being the most aggressive, comprising about 57% of all gliomas 4,5 . Despite aggressive treatments, median survival is only 12-15 months, primarily due to its high recurrence and infiltrative nature 6,7 . Astrocytoma and Oligodendroglioma are characterized by IDH and ATRX mutations and 1p19q co-deletion, respectively 1 .

Techniques like Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) staining and Immunohistochemistry (IHC) are vital for tissue analysis and cancer diagnosis. H&E staining highlights cellular and tissue structures, aiding in tumor subtype identification and grading, while IHC staining, which uses tagged antibodies and detects specific proteins, plays a crucial role in identifying molecular biomarkers 1,8,9 . Integrating deep learning with histopathology offers the potential to predict various biomarkers using H&E stained whole slide images (WSIs). is approach seeks to reduce intra-and inter-observer variability among pathologists and bridge the gap between tumor morphology and genetics, thereby assisting in diagnosis.

In recent years, the field of histopathology has undergone a significant transformation, primarily due to the emergence of digital histopathology 10 . e available datasets like e Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) 11 , IvyGAP 12 , Digital Brain Tumour Atlas (EBRAINS) 13 or TCIA 14 primarily consist of digitized fresh frozen tissue sections. ese types of preparations o en exhibit relatively poor tissue morphology compared to formalin-fixed and paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissues, thus restricting the application of deep learning methods for analysis 15,16 .

e evolution of brain tumor research underscores the importance of incorporating broader demographic datasets, encompassing diverse populations beyond conventional cohorts. is comprehensive understanding, facilitated by datasets from various demographics, helps capture the diversity of cellular and morphological characteristics necessary for further developing deep learning algorithms and extending their applicability to the entire spectrum of brain tumor types.

To address the need for diverse data in brain tumor research, we present the Indian Pathology Brain Dataset (IPD-Brain) containing digitized H&E-stained WSI images of brain tumor from an Indian cohort, each accompanied by relevant clinical data. e thorough manual review process ensures the scan quality and diagnostic accuracy. is dataset contributes to the digital and computational pathology field and makes it a valuable resource for educational purposes. It is specially designed to identify glioma subtypes, WHO grade, and IHC biomarkers such as TP53, ATRX, IDH1, and Ki67 without requiring IHC slides for these markers. TP53 and ATRX are tumor suppressors implicated in glioma formation, IDH1 is involved in metabolic pathways, with its mutations serving as valuable prognostic markers, and Ki67 is a marker for cell proliferation 17 . An overview of data acquisition and deep learning framework, elaborated in the technical validation section, is depicted in Fig. 1.

Moreover, this dataset, coming from a referral tertiary care institute in southern India, is perhaps the largest dataset available in Asia. It is developed to support global collaboration in brain tumor research, enhance diversity among existing cohorts, and provide insights into potential regional and ethnic variations in the disease.

div.head: Data acquisition.
div.p: e IPD-Brain dataset containing H&E stained slides of brain tumors were retrospectively compiled over the period 2019-2023 at Nizam's Institute Of Medical Sciences (NIMS), Hyderabad, a premier tertiary hospital in India. A total of 547 slides from 367 patients were acquired from the hospital archives. Among these, 484 slides from 328 patients were diagnosed with Glioblastoma, Astrocytoma, and Oligodendroglioma. e remaining slides, lacking associated metadata, also pertain to neuropathology. A waiver of consent was given since the data was collected retrospectively. e study was approved by Nizam's Institute of Medical Sciences Institutional Ethics Committee (NIMS-IEC) (reference number: EC/NIMS/2868/2021). e patient's identity information, including pathology case ID numbers, was anonymized, and new case numbers were assigned accordingly to protect the patient's rights and comply with ethical guidelines. All the consecutive adult-type diffuse gliomas were selected from the archival samples. e H&E stained slides, and the diagnosis was reviewed with the help of available immunohistochemistry. e best slide featuring the classic histopathologic feature was selected for scanning. e representative slide was recut from the FFPE tissue block and re-stained to maintain the good quality of the scanned WSI. An experienced pathologist (M.S.U.) supervised this procedure along with the project coordinator (M.K.).

e digitization process was performed with the Morphle DigiPath 6 T Scanner at a 40x magnification, 0.22 microns/pixel, mirroring the detailed observation possible under traditional microscopy. Manual quality control measures were carefully applied to ensure digital representations maintain a high level of accuracy, with the presence of minor artifacts reflecting the natural variability and complexity of real-world cases in the digitization process (refer Technical Validation section for more details). Figure 2 shows the dataset sample for each class and real-world artifacts in our dataset. Exported images were stored in .tiff format at four levels with level downsamples of 1, 4, 16, and 32. Metadata at each level was also exported, and hue & saturation were set to 100, contrast to 66, and brightness to 73 as exportation standard parameters to maintain high color fidelity. is careful approach has created a valuable resource for advancing the understanding of brain tumor pathology.

div.head: Data preprocessing.
div.p: e process begins by segmenting tissue regions within digitized slides. A er smoothing, the image is converted to the HSV color space, and a mask is created by thresholding the saturation channel. Morphological operations fill gaps and holes, and contours are filtered based on area. We have included optimal segmentation parameters in a.csv file in the dataset. Following segmentation, the algorithm crops 256 × 256 patches, as used in 15 , from within the segmented WSI regions based on user-specified magnification without overlap.

Baseline models. In this section, we describe baseline models used for classification tasks on our dataset following the weakly-supervised multiple-instance learning (MIL) framework due to the large size of histopathology images and the lack of patch-level labels in a WSI 18,19 . Unlike traditional supervised learning, which relies on precisely labeled instances (pixel or patch level), MIL operates on 'bags' of instances, with the label determined by the collective characteristics of these instances (slide-level). It is a two-stage framework: (i) Feature extractor and (ii) Feature Aggregator. We benchmarked our dataset using ResNet-50 pre-trained on ImageNet and three domain-specific pre-trained (Histopathology) networks as feature extractors. ese domain-specific pre-trained networks include a ResNet-50 model pre-trained via the Barlow Twins method 20 , a Vision Transformer model pre-trained using the DINO method 21 , and CTransPath, a hybrid model merging a convolutional neural network (CNN) with a multiscale Swin Transformer architecture, pre-trained through semantically-relevant contrastive learning 22 . By incorporating these diverse options, we aimed to comprehensively evaluate their generalizability to the IPD-Brain histopathology dataset.

For feature aggregation, we employed three feature aggregator models, which are described briefly below. ese models were selected based on their performance across various tasks. ey all use attention-based learning to classify WSIs and highlight diagnostically significant sub-regions within the WSIs.

• CLAM 15 : It uses gated attention to assign scores to patches within a whole slide, leveraging these scores for slide-level aggregation through a weighted average for multi-class classification. It operates with n parallel attention branches for n class-specific representations, though studies show the single-branch configuration o en performs better. It incorporates domain knowledge for additional guidance in instance-level clustering. • DSMIL 23 : It employs a dual-stream architecture with self-supervised contrastive learning, for instance, embeddings. One stream identifies the key instance, whereas another aggregates embeddings for a comprehensive bag representation. It uses a unique approach to weight instance contributions based on similarity to the key instance, enhancing the final bag score through an attention mechanism. • DTFD 24 : It generates pseudo-bags from bag divisions, maintaining the original label for each. It utilizes a twotier attention-based MIL model, first estimating pseudo-bag probabilities, then deriving instance probabilities and distilled features for final parent bag likelihood prediction. Despite potential noise, it leverages deep neural network resilience, focusing on Aggregated Feature Selection (AFS) for feature distillation in this context.

Transfer learning for IHC biomarkers. Our investigation sought to evaluate whether H&E stained slides are sufficient to diagnose biomarkers of gliomas (IDH1, ATRX, TP53, and Ki67), which are generally detected by IHC-stained slides. We do so by determining the capability of our MIL deep learning subtype classification model in predicting common diagnostic molecular markers from glioma H&E slides. We also evaluate its potential utility as a clinical secondary check or a cost-effective alternative to molecular biology experiments. Using transfer learning, a technique that adapts a model trained on one task to a related new task, we systematically explored the effectiveness of the best-performing model, initially trained for tumor subtype classification, in inferring molecular biomarkers within a weakly supervised context. Fine-tuning was performed on a model initially trained for subtyping three glioma classes to adapt it for six distinct binary classification tasks. ese tasks involved identifying the presence or absence of somatic mutations in IDH1, TP53, and ATRX genes and evaluating the proliferation of tumor cells using the Ki-67 marker at three cutoff levels commonly applied by pathologists (5%, 10%, 20%).

We adhered to official implementations of the deep learning methods wherever possible, exerting diligent efforts to replicate the code accurately. A comprehensive evaluation was conducted to benchmark our dataset for every combination of feature extractors and aggregators. e dataset was divided into training, validation, and testing sets with proportions of 80%, 10%, and 10%, respectively, on a patient-wise basis.

is approach ensured data leakage prevention, meaning all slides from a single patient were exclusively allocated to one of these sets. Additionally, we implemented a 10-fold cross-validation for each experimental setup.

Training of the models was conducted for a minimum of 50 epochs and a maximum of 200 epochs, with early stopping implemented with a patience of 25 epochs on validation loss. e Adam optimizer was used with a batch size of 1. Specific learning rates and weight decay parameters were set for each aggregator: DSMIL at 2e-4 (learning rate) with a 5e-3 weight decay, CLAM-sb (CLAM) at 2e-4 (learning rate) with a 1e-3 weight decay, and DTFD at 1e-4 (learning rate) with a 1e-4 weight decay. ese parameters were broadly consistent with those defined in the original implementations of these methods. All experiments were performed using Python 3.10.10, Pytorch 2.0.0 + cu117 on RTX 3080ti 12GB GPU. For version details of all the libraries, we have included requirement.txt in GitHub. e dataset details can be accessed through Figshare 25 . e dataset, comprising of high resolution images, can be directly accessed via Data Foundation Portal (https://datafoundation.iiit.ac.in/dataset-versions/cb5917e1-6e56- 4984-b6d1-f91d52ccd36c) under the Healthcare Dataset category (IPD Brain) a er user registration. is process facilitates the easy download and utilization of the dataset by researchers and clinicians interested in brain tumor research, specifically in the study of glioma subtypes. div.head: technical Validation
div.p: Quality control was applied multiple times at different stages. Before digitization, each slide was evaluated using a light microscope to verify staining quality, ensuring digital scans accurately represent the histopathological features necessary for precise analysis. Subsequent scans were reviewed, and suboptimal scans were rescanned, if possible, or excluded. We purposefully include a few WSIs with artifacts of real-world slide imperfections. Clinical annotations, including age, sex, diagnosis, radiology findings, clinical features (C/F), grade, immunohistochemistry (IHC) biomarker statuses (IDH1R132H, ATRX, TP53), and the Ki67 index, were retrieved directly from the patient's records to ensure authenticity and accuracy. To validate the reliability of these annotations, a subset of samples was randomly selected for independent review. is cross-checking process involved confirming the original annotations against the expert diagnosis (M.S.U.), affirming the correctness of labels and diagnoses provided. Such validation of annotations reinforces the dataset's value as a trustworthy resource for training diagnostic models. e primary performance metric used for all the experiments is the Area Under Curve (AUC), which offers a comprehensive assessment and is less susceptible to class imbalance. Additionally, we consider slide-level accuracy (Acc) and the macro-averaged F1 score. ese metrics collectively provide a holistic view of model performance. e AUC score indicates the ability to differentiate between classes, whereas the F1 score offers insight into the actual performance in the context of imbalanced data.

Table 3 shows the IPD-Brain dataset evaluation for the glioma subtype using various deep-learning methods. e combination of ResNet-50 pre-trained on existing available histopathological datasets via the Barlow twin SSL method and the DTFD aggregator performed most effectively among all, achieving an average AUC of 88.08%, an accuracy of 79.83% and an F1 score of 75.87%. Additionally, variation in AUC and F1 scores across 10-folds for all the combinations can be observed in Fig. 4 Figure 5 enhances the interpretability of feature aggregators across glioma subtypes by analyzing attention weights assigned to tissue patches. is visualization highlights critical tissue patches that guide the glioma subtype classification. By employing a gradient scale from blue to red, our model signifies the importance of specific regions within the WSI, with blue indicating regions of lesser significance and red highlighting the most critical areas. In comparison, the traditional manual microscopic examination by neuropathologist in clinical settings is an exhaustive process, requiring extensive scrutiny of the entire slide to identify significant glioma morphological patterns.

e models, trained on our data, were further validated for practical applicability and accuracy through a rigorous single-blind evaluation conducted with an experienced neuropathologist (M.S.U.). e pathologist was presented with the WSI prediction generated by our model. e pathologist scrutinized specific regions within the WSIs to formulate their diagnoses, some of which are shown as 'Raw Patch' in Fig. 5.

By qualitatively analyzing, we can observe DTFD's superior ability to focus on regions indicative of each tumor's clinical characteristics, aligned with known pathological features. e key diagnostic features of glioblastoma, such as microvascular proliferation and palisading necrosis, were accurately highlighted by DTFD. In astrocytoma, the emphasis is on cellular structures devoid of necrosis, showcasing gemistocytic features. e classic histopathologic features of oligodendroglioma, such as the "chicken wire" vascular pattern and "fried egg" appearance of the cells, are also accurately identified. is assessment underlines DTFD's effectiveness in marking diagnostically relevant regions, enhancing model transparency and reliability in histopathological evaluations.

e model demonstrated proficiency in identifying critical morphological microstructures, showing a solid alignment between its focus on important regions and the key areas within the raw WSIs essential for glioma subtype classification. is congruence closely mirrors the diagnostic strategies employed by pathologists, underscoring the model's ability to prioritize and analyze patch segments in a manner similar to how experts identify glioma patterns.

Interestingly, applying stain normalization using StainNet 26 led to a reduction in model performance metrics, with the AUC decreasing from 88.08% to 86.34% and macro F1 score from 75.87% to 70.81%. ese results suggest a minimal presence of stain variability within the IPD-Brain dataset and indicate that the employed feature extractor was capable enough to handle subtle stain variability.

e efficacy of the model in identifying IHC molecular biomarkers (IDH, ATRX, and TP53) is represented in Table 4. ese results highlight the potential of the model in identifying molecular biomarkers using H&E slides. Moreover, the model shows remarkable performance in classifying the Ki67 at various cutoffs (Table 5), which is crucial for assessing tumor cell proliferation rates. e optimal cutoff value was observed as 10%, achieving an AUC of 89.55% and an F1 score of 91.17%. is level of performance in IDH1R132H and Ki67 classification emphasizes the model's accuracy and practical utility in providing essential prognostic information necessary for effective treatment planning and patient management.

In conclusion, this dataset is a technically validated resource, characterized by its detailed annotation, high-quality image preparation, and the performance of deep learning methods in classifying glioma subtypes, grades, and, IHC biomarkers. Future efforts will focus on adding survival and treatment data, offering a more comprehensive understanding of patient outcomes. We also plan to leverage pathomics 27 to investigate the relationship between morphological features and phenotypes, providing deeper insights into how these characteristics influence disease diagnosis, progression, and treatment responses. Additionally, since the dataset includes radiological reports, further studies can be carried out to integrate radiological findings, morphological features and clinical data to improve diagnostic accuracy and predicting patient's outcomes.

All the 547 WSIs included in this dataset have been saved as standard tiff format images. e corresponding clinical data is provided in a spreadsheet file, available through the Figshare 25 . is dataset can be combined with other datasets for training machine learning models and for educational purposes. Despite its valuable applications, the dataset has limitations. ere is a class imbalance that can affect the training and generalization of machine learning models. While the dataset includes labels for IHC biomarkers, it lacks the actual IHC slides, which may limit its utility for certain types of molecular marker analysis. Additionally, all images were captured using a single scanner at a single site, which may limit the generalizability of machine learning models developed only with this dataset. Acknowledging these limitations is essential for researchers planning to use this dataset. Table 5. Ki-67 as classification task results.

Digitization of the WSI is then obtained, and QC of the same is done.
